topicName: N-gram Language Models and Smoothing Techniques

[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"N-gram Language Models and Smoothing Techniques"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Language Modeling"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"A language model computes the probability of a sequence of words. Given a sequence of words W = w_1, w_2, ..., w_n, we want to assign a probability P(W). Language models are fundamental in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for tasks such as machine translation, speech recognition, and text generation."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"The N-gram Approach and the Markov Assumption"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"Computing the exact probability of an entire sentence directly is difficult due to data sparsity. To simplify this, we use the chain rule of probability along with the Markov assumption. An N-gram model assumes that the probability of a word depends only on the preceding N-1 words."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Unigram (N=1): P(w_1, w_2, ..., w_n) = product of P(w_i)"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Bigram (N=2): P(w_i | w_1, ..., w_{i-1}) approx P(w_i | w_{i-1})"},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Trigram (N=3): P(w_i | w_1, ..., w_{i-1}) approx P(w_i | w_{i-2}, w_{i-1})"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Parameters for N-gram models are typically estimated using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). We count the frequencies of N-grams in a large text corpus and normalize them."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"def calculate_bigram_probability(bigram_count, unigram_count):
    if unigram_count == 0:
        return 0.0
    return bigram_count / unigram_count"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"The Zero Probability Problem"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"MLE fails when encountering valid N-grams that were not present in the training corpus. If a specific bigram count is zero, the entire sentence probability becomes zero. Smoothing techniques are required to redistribute probability mass to unseen events."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Smoothing Technique 1: Laplace (Add-One) Smoothing"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Laplace smoothing is the simplest technique. It pretends we have seen every possible N-gram at least once by adding 1 to all N-gram counts and adjusting the vocabulary denominator."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"def laplace_smoothing(bigram_count, unigram_count, vocab_size):
    return (bigram_count + 1) / (unigram_count + vocab_size)"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Smoothing Technique 2: Good-Turing Estimation"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Good-Turing smoothing re-estimates the counts of N-grams based on the frequency of N-grams that occur r times. It assigns probability mass to unseen items (r=0) using the count of items that appeared only once (N_1)."},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Smoothing Technique 3: Interpolation and Backoff"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"Interpolation combines the probability estimates of trigrams, bigrams, and unigrams by mixing them linearly with weights that sum to 1. Backoff relies on higher-order N-grams if available, and falls back to lower-order models only when the higher-order count is zero."},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"def interpolate(p_tri, p_bi, p_uni, lambda_weights):
    l1, l2, l3 = lambda_weights
    return (l3 * p_tri) + (l2 * p_bi) + (l1 * p_uni)"},{"order":22,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":23,"type":"paragraph","text":"While modern NLP heavily relies on neural language models like Transformers, N-grams with robust smoothing techniques remain important baselines for efficient text modeling, spell checking, and keyword extraction."}]
